content: Infection with the bacterium Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) can lead to severe illnesses such as meningitis, pneumonia, bacteremia, cellulitis, septic arthritis, and epiglottitis. These infections primarily affect infants and children under the age of five. Haemophilus influenzae is a non-motile, Gram-negative coccobacillus that was first identified in 1892 by Richard Pfeiffer during an influenza pandemic. Although it was initially thought to be the causative agent of influenza, this was disproven in 1933 when the viral origin of influenza was discovered. Despite this, H. influenzae remains a significant pathogen, causing a variety of clinical diseases. The bacterium is generally aerobic but can also grow as a facultative anaerobe. Transmission occurs through direct contact with respiratory droplets from an infected individual or a carrier. In the United States, the incidence of invasive Hib disease among children under five years of age was between 40 and 100 cases per 100,000 children during the 1980s. However, since the introduction of the Hib conjugate vaccine in 1990, the incidence has dramatically decreased to approximately 1.3 cases per 100,000 children. In contrast, in developing countries where the vaccine is not widely available, Hib remains a leading cause of lower respiratory tract infections in infants and children. Certain groups are at higher risk of acquiring Hib infection. These include infants, young children, household contacts of infected individuals, and children who attend daycare. The prognosis for Hib infections varies. Between 3% and 6% of cases are fatal, and up to 20% of survivors may experience long-term complications, such as permanent hearing loss or other sequelae. Before the widespread use of the Hib conjugate vaccine, more than half of Hib cases in industrialized countries presented as meningitis, characterized by symptoms such as fever, headache, and stiff neck. Other cases manifested as cellulitis, arthritis, or sepsis. In developing countries, Hib continues to be a major cause of bacterial pneumonia-related deaths in children. Treatment of invasive Hib disease requires specific parenteral antibiotic therapy. In cases of epiglottitis, immediate stabilization of the airway is critical. A four-day course of rifampin is effective in eradicating Hib carriage from the pharynx in approximately 95% of carriers. The primary method of prevention is vaccination with the Hib conjugate vaccine. This vaccine has significantly reduced the incidence of invasive Hib disease in countries where it is routinely administered. Future research is focused on improving the characteristics of Hib vaccines to enhance their ability to prevent both invasive disease and bacterial carriage. These advancements could also inform the development of conjugate vaccines for other encapsulated bacteria, such as Neisseria meningitidis (meningococcus), Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus), and group B streptococcus. Additionally, further studies on herd immunity effects may provide insights into optimizing vaccination strategies to prevent both disease and transmission of H. influenzae.
